https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/cou.text: The Budapest Times Court clears path for tyranny, says opposition party Today's ruling by the "beheaded and intimidated" Constitutional Court opens the door to further steps toward tyranny, the Fidesz parliamentary faction said in response to the Constitutional Court's rejection of the joint petition filed by Fidesz and KDNP seeking the annulment of the 16th and 17th amendments to the Basic Law. In a statement titled “Tyranny Is Being Built Brick by Brick,” the opposition party wrote that if the president of the republic can be removed through legislation tailored to a specific individual, then in today’s Hungary, the Tisza majority can do anything to anyone. “Fidesz will continue its peaceful and lawful resistance to tyranny and will make use of every available means, both inside and outside parliament,” the statement read. Fidesz and KDNP challenged certain provisions of the 16th and 17th amendments to the Basic Law through a post-enactment norm-control procedure. The opposition alliance requested the annulment of the provision that terminated Tamás Sulyok’s mandate as president of the republic with immediate effect. They also initiated the annulment of the amendment introducing a time limit on the eligibility of members of parliament to stand for election, which stipulates that a person who has already served as a member of parliament for at least twelve years or through three terms may not obtain a parliamentary mandate. The opposition alliance also challenged the Basic Law amendment relating to Constitutional Court justices, which reinstated the upper age limit of seventy years for judges. The Constitutional Court announced on 14 August that it had rejected the petition submitted by Fidesz and the KDNP, in which the party had requested the annulment of the article concerning public-interest asset management foundations performing public duties, contained in the 16th amendment to the Basic Law. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: Some 100 schools have been severely damaged during French high school protests that escalated this week into “urban violence,” with 40 headteachers injured, according to the latest figures from the French education ministry. The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said. During a call with local prosecutors last night, the justice minister Gérald Darmanin urged them to pursue civil liability claims so that parents are made financially responsible for damage caused by their children.
